The Story of Nagdatt the Dharma-Lover

I bow to Lord Jina, the bestower of all happiness, and I write the story of Nagdatt, who loved dharma.

Dharmapal was king of Ujjain. His queen was Dharmashri, a righteous and very generous woman. In that city lived a merchant named Sagardatt, whose wife was Subhadra. They had a son named Nagdatt. Like his mother, Nagdatt too was a lover of dharma. He had unwavering faith in dharma. His marriage to Priyangushri, the beautiful daughter of merchant Samudradatt, was celebrated with great pomp. Much charity was given, worship and festivals were performed, and the poor and distressed were generously helped.

Priyangushri was desired by her cousin Nagasen, but Sagardatt had married her to Nagdatt. This greatly displeased Nagasen. So he developed enmity toward poor Nagdatt and began looking for an opportunity to harm him.

One day, Nagdatt was standing in kayotsarga meditation at the Jain temple, absorbed in dharma-love. Nagasen spotted him. The wicked one devised a conspiracy to take revenge for his enmity. He took off his necklace from his own neck and placed it near Nagdatt's feet, then raised an alarm: 'This man was stealing my necklace and running away. I chased and caught him. Now he's pretending to meditate so he won't be caught.' Hearing Nagasen's alarm, many people gathered, and the police arrived too. Nagdatt was arrested and brought to the royal court. The king, finding no proof in Nagdatt's favour, ordered him to be executed.

Nagdatt was immediately taken to the execution ground. The sword stroke that was meant to cut off his head felt to him as if someone had thrown a garland of flowers upon him. He was not hurt at all, and at that very moment, flowers rained down from the sky upon him. The sky resounded with cries of 'Victory! Well done!' Everyone who saw this miracle was amazed. Truly, who does not help the noble souls, the patient great ones, who are devoted to dharma?

Seeing the blissful power of Jain dharma in this way, Nagdatt and King Dharmapal were both greatly pleased. They now renounced all worldly attachment for the sake of the happiness of liberation, took Jain initiation, and became monks. Many others too were inspired by this miracle and embraced Jain dharma.

This story teaches that those who are truly devoted to dharma are protected by its power. Nagdatt, though falsely accused and sentenced to death, was unharmed by the sword and honoured by the gods. His unwavering faith and innocence saved him. The wise should practise dharma with sincerity, for dharma protects those who protect it.
